title: CNN Part 3 | Convolution Operation
full_text: Hi guys, my name is Nitesh and welcome  to my YouTube channel. In this video,  we will continue our deep learning  playlist. In deep learning, we are  studying Convolutional Neural Networks,  and we have covered two videos so far  where I explained the basics of CNN and  its biological connection to our visual  cortex. Now, starting from today's  video, we will begin to study CNN in  great detail. We will study the  components within it one by one. And in  today's video, we are going to study  its most important component. What is a  convolution operation? If you  understand this operation, you won't  have much trouble understanding CNNs.  Right? So, let's start the video. We  will start this video from our current  understanding of CNN. So, we know so  far that a CNN is just a neural network . It's a neural network. It's a special  neural network whose architecture is  slightly different from ANN. Right?  Because here you will see some  different types of layers. One of these  is the convolution layer, which we are  going to look at in this video. Apart  from this, there is a pooling layer,  and then there is a fully connected  layer, which you also call a dense  layer in ANN terms. So, our CNN is made  up of these three types of layers. Now,  we have learned about CNN that it works  very well with images. And this is  because the architecture and working  principle of CNN are based on our own  visual cortex. So, I will summarize for  you exactly how a CNN works. Let's take  a high-level overview. So, you can  roughly understand that this is a CNN  where the initial layers are your  convolution layers, and from here, this  part is the fully connected layer. So,  what happens is that as soon as you  feed an image into a CNN, the initial  layers perform edge detection. They  find the edges in the given image.  Because if you think about it, any  image is made up of edges. So, you can  call them primitive features. So, the  job of our initial layers is to detect  edges within our given image. And then,  as you go deeper into this network, the  job of the subsequent convolution  layers is to combine those edges to  generate slightly more complex features , and then gradually you move forward  to perform tasks like classification.  Right? So the idea is very simple: the  initial layers will find primitive  features, like edges. The following  layers will find slightly more complex  features, and by continuing to add  these up, we reach the end and identify  things completely. Right? If you take  the example of face detection, your  face is made up of edges. From edges,  you are gradually creating complex  patterns. Such as eyes, nose, and ears.  And then, by putting these together,  you start forming a complete face. And  then, using that complete face, you  identify whether the user is the one we  are looking for or not. So, this is the  overall idea of CNN. And clearly, the  most important component here is this  convolution layer, these layers, right?  We will see their main usage in this  video. The target of our video today is  to understand the convolution operation  inside and out. As soon as you  understand this, you will have grasped  the very first thing required for CNN.  Now, to understand this video, you need  to be well-versed in one concept, and  that is: what images are and how they  are stored in computer memory. Right?  So we will talk about two types of  images. The first type is a grayscale  image. Which you call a black and white  image. And the second is an RGB image,  which you call a colored image. We  mostly work with these two types of  images. So first, let me show you an  example of how a grayscale image is  stored in memory. For instance, this is  an image of a zero from the MNIST  dataset, and this is a very  low-resolution image. Meaning 28x28  pixels. So an image is basically made  up of pixels. You can imagine a grid  like this. You can imagine a grid of  28x28 like this, and each grid  represents a number between 0 to 255; 0  means black, 255 means white. Right,  sometimes you normalize this to a range  of 0 to 1, where 0 means black and 1  means white. So you can see, this is  exactly what I have shown here. If you  zoom out, you would see that this image  is basically a collection of 28x28  pixels. Right? And here you can see the  value of every pixel. All these pixels  have a value of zero. It should have  been one because it is white. But you  can understand it is slightly flipped.  It is inverted. Okay? Then when you  come here, these pixels have a value of  one. Moving here, it is a slight gray  shade. That is why it is point two. But  you get the idea. Whenever you look at  pixels, uh, whenever you look at any  image, you can imagine it in such a way  that it is basically a collection of  pixels. You can store this in a 2D  array. And that is what our computers  do. When you tell them to process  images, what they are actually  processing is 2D NumPy arrays. Okay? So , this was about grayscale images or  black and white images. Now I will show  you what happens with colored images.  So, a colored image actually has three  channels. Okay? And those three  channels are red, green, and blue.  Basically our primary colors, using  which you can create any other color.  Okay? So whenever you see any RGB image  or a colored image, it is actually made  up of three channels. Uh, this is the  top red channel, behind it is the green , and behind that is the blue channel.  Okay? And each of these sheets, every  sheet will act like a single grayscale  image. Okay? Here, there will be values  only from zero to 255. This one will  also have values from zero to 255. And  here too, there will be values only  from zero to 255. And generally, their  shape will be something like 228 by 228  by 3. So now let's discuss the most  fundamental building block of a CNN,  which is the convolution operation. So,  the job of the convolution operation is  to extract features from an image. And  I told you that the initial layers  detect edges. So now I will show you  the convolution operation using edge  detection. We will see how the  convolution operation works in edge  detection. Okay? So, let me first show  you what the output of edge detection  looks like. Let's assume this is an  image. This is a grayscale image, black  and white. And we performed two types  of edge detection on it. First, we did  an edge detection which was vertical  edge detection. And you can see clearly  here that all the vertical edges in  this image are visible in the first one . And then we did another edge  detection for horizontal edges. So you  can see that we have all the horizontal  edges in this picture. Similarly, you  can also perform slant edge detection.  You can detect any kind of edge. Okay?  So the output will look like this. Now  I am going to show you. How you achieve  this mathematically. Also, if someone  asks you what edges are. It's a very  simple thing. Edges are basically a  change in intensity. Like, look here,  this whole area is black. But when you  come here, the pixels are turning white . So this is your edge. Because the  intensity is changing here. Similarly,  you can say the intensity is changing  here too. The intensity is changing  here as well. So having edges means  intensity change. So now we have to  mathematically detect the edges somehow . We need to detect the intensity  change. Because with the human eye, you  can easily understand that yes, there  is an edge. But how will an algorithm  detect this? We are about to see the  beauty of that. That is where the  convolution operation is used. So I am  going to show you a very small example.  Where we have a 6x6, very  low-resolution image. And we will  perform edge detection on it. You can  see all the pixels at the top are zero.  Which means they are black, and all the  bottom pixels are white. So this image  will look something like this. This  image will look something like this.  Okay? So we have to perform edge  detection on this. We need to find out  where the intensity is changing and  obviously the output should be like  this. This should be the output. This  is our input. This should be the output . Okay? So how will we do it? So to  perform a convolution operation, you  need something called a filter. In some  places, it is also called a kernel.  This is basically a matrix and  generally its size is 3x3, but it can  be larger. Like this is a 3x3 filter.  Okay? It is basically a matrix of  numbers. Here, the filter we are using  will act as a horizontal edge detector.  Meaning, it can detect all the  horizontal edges present in your  picture. Now, what will we do? We will  take this filter and convolve it over  this image. Now, this sign here is for  the convolution operator. Okay? How  does the convolution operation work? I  will explain in a while. But as soon as  you convolve, you get a result, and  this result is called a feature map.  Okay? So image, filter, feature map— there are three things here. Okay? Now,  let's start our discussion on how the  convolution operation works. So for the  convolution operation, you first pick  up this filter, and place it on top of  this image at the top-left like this.  You picked it up and placed it on top.  And now what will you do? You perform  element-wise multiplication. Meaning,  you multiply this number with this one.  This one with this one. This one with  this one. This one with this one. This  one with this one. And so on. And then  you add up all these multiplications.  So basically, it would look like this.  -1*0 + -1*0 + -1*0, then second row,  then third row; the number obtained  after adding will go into this cell. As  you can see here, all the numbers are  zero, so zero will go into this cell.  This was step one. Now, what will you  do? Now you will move your filter  slightly to the right and bring it here  to this spot. And you will do the same  thing. Again, the result was zero. Then  you move further to this spot. Again,  the result was zero. And in the end,  you move one more step forward and  again the result was zero. Okay? So we  have run the convolution over our first  row. Now, what will we do? We will move  one row down. So we will come here to  this spot. Okay? Now, look at what  happens here; this first row will  become zero. The second row will also  become zero. But in the third one, 255* 1 + 255*1 + 255*1, so a large number  will appear. But we know that the  largest number possible is 255. So 255  will come here. Okay? Then we will move  forward a bit. We'll grab this. Again,  255 will come here. Then we will move  ahead. 255. You can pause the video and  check the calculation. 255 and this row  is done too. Okay? I'll clear  everything once. And now I'll show you  what's next. Now we will start from  here next. Okay? This time this row is  all zero. This is also all zero and  this one is 255 again. Then we will  move here. This is also 255. This is  255 and this is 255 too. Okay? Then  this one is also finished. Now we will  come to the last three rows. Okay? In  this case, look, these -1 s make all  these negative 255. The middle one all  becomes zero and these all become  positive 255. So you can easily do the  calculation, it will be zero. So it  moved as zero here, zero here, zero  here, zero here. Okay? And now look  guys, how our feature map looks. Zero  on top, zero on bottom. In the middle,  you have 255 values. So basically it  would look something like this. Right,  you can see this is what we wanted and  we got it. So this is called edge  detection. This is an example of  horizontal edge detection. But if you  change the filters, like this filter.  If you change its values, then you can  get different types of edge detectors.  Like if you have these values. If you  have these values, then this will act  as a vertical edge detector. You can  pause the video and try it out if you  want. This filter will work as a  vertical edge detector. In the same way , what will happen? You can use other  values to detect slanted edges. You can  detect edges of this kind. So computer  scientists have created many types of  filters. Right filter, left filter, top  filter, bottom filter. So you can use  any filter. But the good part is, the  best thing is that in deep learning,  you don't need to worry about what the  filter value will be. Okay? What  happens in deep learning is that you  train these filters. You initialize it  with a random value, and then your CNN  automatically decides through  backpropagation what the values should  be. So in short, these filter values  behave exactly like weights in an ANN.  In an ANN, the values of the weights  are determined during training.  Similarly, what these values in the  filters will be is also determined  after we train. Depending on the image  and depending on the training data. So  in short, we don't need to worry. We  just need to define these matrices. The  rest of the work is handled by  backpropagation. We don't need to  create the filters ourselves. And this  is one of the main reasons why CNNs  have been so successful. Because it  doesn't rely on pre-made filters. It  can create filters on the go according  to its requirements. Okay? But all these blue  values, since they are negative, will  be replaced by zero. So you can imagine  that the remaining image, the feature  map we have, will only have the left  edge. Okay? So when  we start convolving it over this volume , we will first take the 27 values here . Okay? So basically, 27 values are  being element-wise multiplied with 27  values and then added. So basically,  when you place this filter here for the  first time, you are getting one number  which will come for this box. Then you  move this way, then another number,  another number, and another number.  Then you come down, and you start  getting its corresponding numbers. That  is why when you convolve a  three-channel image with a  three-channel filter, you get a  single-channel feature map. So you must  always remember that when you convolve  an m cross m cross channel with an n  cross n cross channel filter, you get  an m-n + 1 cross m-n + 1 single-channel  feature map. This is the biggest  learning here. I hope you have  understood this whole thing. So now, in  this video, we will discuss one last  thing: what happens if you apply  multiple filters to the same image. So  honestly, this happens very rarely. In  fact, it never happens that you only  apply a single filter to your image.  Generally, you apply more filters, more  than one filter. Okay? So for example,  suppose you can imagine that you have  applied two filters and the first  filter will perform vertical edge  detection. The second one will perform  horizontal edge detection. There could  be a third filter that performs slant  edge detection. Meaning, it depends.  Okay? So you have to understand what  will happen in this case. So, by now  you must have understood that when you  perform a 3x3 convolution on a 6x6x3  input, you will get this 4x4 feature  map, so with one filter you will be  getting one feature map. If you have  two filters, then you will get another  feature map of the same dimension. If  there were three filters, one more  feature map would be obtained. If there  were 10 filters, 10 feature maps would  be obtained. And now, if you have two  feature maps, you can treat them like a  volume, like this. So here, your  resultant shape is 4x4x2, and you can  imagine it as a volume that will act as  input for further convolution layers.  Okay? I hope you are understanding this  point. Okay? If you had 10 filters,  then your resultant would be 4x4x10. So , basically, this number here is the  number of filters used. The number of  filters you use is the number of  channels you will have in your output.  Okay? I hope things are clear up to  this point. So that's it for the video,  guys.
